newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia issues guides for foreign investors.
newsitem.headline: Croatia issues guides for foreign investors.

text.p: Croatia, aiming this year to attract double last year's direct foreign investment, on Monday issued an economic outlook for 1997 and a legal framework for doing businness in Croatia.

The books, published in English, are designed to give potential foreign investors information on the country's economic structure and macroeconomic data, and a digest guide through its business legislation.
"These two books are exactly what we needed: comprehensive surveys which bring all the important data into one place," Economics Minister Davor Stern said at the presentation.
Direct foreign investments in Croatia doubled to $280 million in 1996, according to the National Bank of Croatia, and Stern said he expected the figure to double again in 1997.
"We have to be more aggressive in attracting foreign capital, and these publications are a step forward in that direction," Stern said.

"Croatia -- Economic Outlook 1997" contains a detailed description of the economy, its current and expected growth, basics of monetary and fiscal policies, balance of payments, prices trends and employment figures from 1993 to 1999.
The data were compiled from various official sources, including the central bank, the State Statistics Bureau, Zagrebacka Banka and also foreign sources including the leading credit rating agencies.
According to the data, the economy is expected to grow between 5.0 and 6.5 percent per year in real terms till 1999, with inflation remaining in the 3.3-3.5 percent range.
Velimir Sonje, executive director for analysis at the NBC, who took part in compiling the outlook, said a stable macroeconomic environment was expected over the next three years.
"We don't envisage any changes in the main elements of macroeconomic policy -- low inflation, stable exchange rate and a prosperous economy," Sonje said.
The other book, "Legal Framework for Doing Business in Croatia", is a 157-page user-friendly guide through the Croatian legal system, said to be among the region's most liberal.

"Croatia is completely open for foreign investments, it is one of the few countries that has a so-called 'national treatment' of foreigners, and guarantees for investments built into the constitution," said the chief editor, Branko Vukmir.

Jaksa Barbic, a university professor and one of the authors of the key company law, said Croatia had gone further down the road towards meeting Western legal standards than its emerging market neighbours, especially other countries that emerged from the break-up of the former Yugoslavia.
"Whatever you can do in the West in legal terms, you can do in Croatia," Barbic said, adding that the main problem with the Croatian legal framework was its implementation.
